files.lesson.md: --- order: 58 unit: twoway10 node: [AC9M10ST04 n1, AC9M10ST04 n2] uses: ["AC9M8P02 n1", "AC9M7N06 n3"] connection: survey-two-way title: "Row or column percentages" summary: "Counts mislead when groups are different sizes. Turn each row (or column) into a percentage of its own total, then compare, and say which group each percentage is of." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "More bus and car students play sport than riders do. So are bus and car students more sporty?" --- A school (made up) asked 200 Year 10 students how they get to school and whether they play a sport. The answers went into a **two-way table**. Look at the counts and make a guess before any working. ## Predict: counts or chances ```step stage: predict insight: "Choosing who is most likely to play sport from raw counts shows whether students compare groups by how many, or by what fraction of each group." check: type: predict q: "Which group is most likely to play sport: students who ride, walk, or come by bus or car?" options: - "Bus or car, because the most of them play sport (40)" - "Walk, because 33 of 60 is more than half" - "Ride, because 30 of the 40 riders play sport" - "They are all the same" actual: "Riders. 30 of 40 is 75%, walkers are 55% and bus or car students are 40%. The bus and car group has the most players only because it is the biggest group." ``` Make a guess before you check. ## Run: reading the table ```step stage: run insight: "Reading a row and its total is the first move: the total of the row is the size of the group, and it is the number a percentage is taken of." check: type: number q: "How many walkers are in the survey in all? (Read the Total column.)" answer: 60 tolerance: 0 feedback: - [33, "That is the walkers who play sport. The total counts the walkers who play sport and those who do not."] explain: "33 play sport and 27 do not, so there are 60 walkers in all." ``` Each row is one group of students: 30 + 10 = 40 riders, 33 + 27 = 60 walkers, 40 + 60 = 100 bus or car. The three groups are different sizes, which is why the counts alone can't answer the question. ## Investigate: a percentage of its own group ```step stage: investigate insight: "Dividing by the group's own total (the row) answers 'how likely is someone in this group'. Dividing by the grand total or by the wrong total answers a different question." tasks: - hint: ["Divide by the walkers, not by everyone.", "33 ÷ 60, then × 100."] check: type: number q: "What percentage of the walkers play sport?" answer: 55 tolerance: 0.05 feedback: - [16.5, "That divides by all 200 students. The question is about the walkers, so divide by the 60 walkers."] explain: "33 ÷ 60 = 0.55, which is 55%. Out of the walkers, 55% play sport." smaller: check: type: number q: "Of 60 walkers, 33 play sport. What is 33 ÷ 60 as a decimal?" answer: 0.55 tolerance: 0.005 explain: "33 ÷ 60 = 0.55. Multiply by 100 to make it a percentage." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#dev" text: "Dev works out the percentage of walkers who play sport. Click the line where he goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: percent-of-grand-total explain: "Line 3: Dev divides by all 200 students. The walkers are a group of 60, so he should work out 33 out of 60. His 16.5% is the share of all students who both walk and play sport." - check: type: question q: "Riders: 30 of 40 play sport. Bus or car: 40 of 100. Which comparison is fair?" options: ["75% of riders against 40% of bus or car students, because each is a percentage of its own group", "30 against 40, because the more the better", "30 against 100, because 100 is the biggest total", "Riders can't be compared with bus or car students"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Counts depend on how big each group is. The bus or car group is two and a half times as big as the riders.", "That mixes a count with a group total.", "They can be compared, once each is a percentage of its own group."] explain: "Groups of different sizes are compared by percentages of their own totals. 75% of riders play sport and 40% of bus or car students." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#mia" text: "Mia wants the percentage of riders who play sport. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: wrong-way-percentage explain: "Line 3: Mia divides by 103, everyone who plays sport. That gives the share of players who ride, a different question. For the percentage of riders who play sport, divide by the 40 riders." ``` ### One row's percentage Here is how to work out a row percentage. ```worked \text{Pick the group, a row} :: The question says walkers, so use the Walk row. \text{The row total is the whole group} :: 33 + 27 = 60 walkers. \frac{33}{60} = 0.55 :: Count in the cell divided by the row total. 0.55 \times 100 = 55\% :: Turn it into a percentage and say it: 55% of walkers play sport. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Dev's working. What is the percentage actually of? ### A fair comparison ### Which way? Read Mia's working. Which total should she have divided by? ## Modify: other cells, other directions ```step stage: modify insight: "Filling a missing cell from the totals, taking a row percentage for the other column, and a column percentage shows the two directions answer different questions." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A different survey (made up): there are 80 students who take part in a club. 52 of them are in Year 10. In the club, how many are not in Year 10? (Fill the missing cell: row total minus the cell.)" answer: 28 tolerance: 0 feedback: - [52, "That is the Year 10 cell. The missing cell is the rest of the row total."] explain: "80 − 52 = 28 are not in Year 10." - check: type: number q: "In the bus-or-car row, 60 of the 100 students do not play sport. What percentage of bus or car students do not play sport?" answer: 60 tolerance: 0 feedback: - [40, "That is the percentage who do play sport. The question asks about those who do not."] explain: "60 ÷ 100 = 0.6, so 60%. Row percentages add to 100%: 40% play sport and 60% do not." - check: type: number q: "Now go down a column. Of the 103 students who play sport, 30 ride. What percentage of the players ride? (1 decimal place)" answer: 29.1 tolerance: 0.05 feedback: - [75, "That is the percentage of riders who play sport. This question divides by the 103 players."] explain: "30 ÷ 103 = 0.291, so about 29.1%. It says 'of the players, 29.1% ride', a different thing from 'of the riders, 75% play'." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: a group has only 4 students, and 3 of them play sport (75%). Is that as strong a sign as the 75% of the 40 riders?" options: ["No: with only 4 students, one student changes the percentage a lot, so be careful about reading much into it", "Yes: 75% is 75%", "Yes: the smaller the group the better", "No: percentages can't be used on small groups"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The percentage is the same, but 4 students is a very small group. One more student who did not play sport would drop it to 60%.", "A small group varies a lot, so it tells you less.", "You can work the percentage out. Just be careful how much you read into it."] explain: "A percentage from a very small group can swing with one student. 30 of 40 is much firmer evidence than 3 of 4." ``` ### Missing cell ### The other column ### Down a column ### A small group ## Practise: fair comparisons ```step stage: practise insight: "Row percentages from counts, picking the group with the highest rate, and (review) a percentage of an amount." tasks: - check: type: number q: "In the survey, what percentage of the bus or car students play sport?" answer: 40 tolerance: 0 explain: "40 ÷ 100 = 0.4, which is 40%." - check: type: question q: "Which group has the highest percentage playing sport: ride (30 of 40), walk (33 of 60) or bus or car (40 of 100)?" options: ["Ride, 75%", "Walk, 55%", "Bus or car, 40%", "Bus or car, because 40 is the most players"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Walk is 55%, which is less than 75%.", "Bus or car is the lowest rate, 40%.", "40 players is the biggest count, not the biggest percentage of a group."] explain: "30 ÷ 40 = 75%, 33 ÷ 60 = 55%, 40 ÷ 100 = 40%. Riders have the highest percentage." - check: type: number q: "Review: a club has $80$ members and $45\\%$ are in Year 10. How many members is that?" answer: 36 tolerance: 0 explain: "45% of 80 = 0.45 × 80 = 36." ``` ### Bus or car ### Highest rate ### Review From earlier years: a percentage of an amount. ## Make: your own comparison ```step stage: make insight: "Writing a sentence that names its group, with the right percentage, shows they can report a row percentage and compare two groups fairly." tasks: - hint: ["Subtract the two percentages.", "75 − 55."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "In the school survey, $75\\%$ of riders play sport and $55\\%$ of walkers play sport. By how many percentage points is the riders' percentage higher?" steps: - ["$30 \\div 40 = 0.75$", "the riders' row percentage"] - ["$33 \\div 60 = 0.55$", "the walkers' row percentage"] - ["$75 - 55 = 20$", "the difference, in percentage points"] answer: "20" answerLabel: "Percentage points higher" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["3", "That is the difference in the counts, 33 − 30. Compare the percentages instead."] - ["27", "Check the subtraction: 75 − 55."] criteria: - "I used a row percentage for each group." - "I subtracted the two percentages." - "I said what each percentage is of." explain: "75% − 55% = 20 percentage points. 75% of riders play sport and 55% of walkers do." - check: type: question q: "Which sentence reports the table correctly?" options: ["75% of the students who ride play sport, and 55% of the students who walk do", "75% of the students play sport", "75% of the sport players ride", "Riders play more sport than anyone, so riding makes you sporty"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "75% is the percentage of riders. It is not the percentage of all students.", "That reverses the direction. 75% is the percentage of riders who play, not of players who ride.", "The table shows a link. It can't show that riding is the reason."] explain: "A row percentage names its group: 'of the students who ride'. It says what the table shows and no more." ``` ### How many points higher Work this out on paper first, then type your answer. ### The sentence All the figures in this lesson are made up: the school, the 200 students and their travel and sport. **Also used in** - **News and surveys.** 'Women are twice as likely...' claims are about a percentage of each group; always ask 'percentage of what?'. - **Health.** Rates in a two-way table, such as vaccinated or not against caught the illness or not, are compared by row percentages. - **Next lesson.** A careful claim: what the table lets you say about a link, and what it doesn't. ```teacher summary: Students compare groups of different sizes with row percentages, and learn to say what each percentage is of. The context is how Year 10 students travel to school and whether they play sport, with made-up survey counts (AC9M10ST04, nodes 1 and 2). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 17 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can fill in a two-way table and check its totals. - I can work out a row percentage and say what group it is a percentage of. - I can tell a row percentage from a column percentage. struggle: Choosing which total to divide by. Ask 'which group is the question about?' and point at that row before they touch the calculator. before: > Do the Investigate tasks yourself. The table is 200 Year 10 students (made up): Ride 30 play sport and 10 do not (40), Walk 33 and 27 (60), Bus or car 40 and 60 (100). 103 play sport in all. The one idea: a percentage needs a whole. Row percentages divide by the row total, so they compare the groups (75%, 55%, 40%). Column percentages divide by the column total and answer a different question: of the 103 players, 29.1% ride, 32.0% walk and 38.8% come by bus or car. The common slips: dividing by the grand total (Dev: 33 ÷ 200 = 16.5%), dividing by the other total (Mia: 30 ÷ 103), and choosing the group with the biggest count. All three come from not asking 'percentage of what?'. Every figure is made up. The pairing of travel to school and sport is invented for the lesson; no real survey is quoted. If you want real data, the Australian Bureau of Statistics publishes how Australians travel to work, but none of it is used here. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands before looking at any percentage. Students who pick 'bus or car' have compared counts." - "Investigate: ask students to say each percentage in a full sentence beginning 'Of the...'." - "Modify: the small group edge case is the start of 'how much to trust it'. Ask what one extra student would change." stuck: - see: A student divides by 200 every time (Dev's mistake). ask: Which group is the question about? How many students are in it? fix: Circle the row, read its total, and divide by that number. - see: A student gets 29% for the riders (Mia's mistake). ask: Who is the 103? Who is the 40? fix: 103 is everyone who plays sport. The question is about riders, so use the Ride row's total, 40. - see: A student says bus or car is the most sporty because 40 is the biggest number. ask: How many students are in that group compared with the riders? fix: Counts depend on group size. Change each count to a percentage of its own group. stretch: Write a column percentage sentence and a row percentage sentence for the same cell, and say which question each one answers. support: Give a table with the row totals circled and the sentence 'Of the ___ who ___, ___% ___'. Fill the blanks together for the walkers. leads: > Next: A careful claim. A row percentage shows a link between travel and sport; it doesn't say that the way they travel is the reason. Where it leads in class: students take a table from the news and report what the percentages show and what they do not. exit: q: In a survey, 18 of the 30 students in Year 9 are in a band, and 24 of the 60 students in Year 10. Which year has the higher percentage in a band? a: "Year 9: 18 ÷ 30 = 60%, against 24 ÷ 60 = 40% for Year 10." explain: > A percentage needs a whole, and a row percentage uses the row total as the whole. - Pick the group the question is about: that is the row. - Divide the cell by the row total. - Say it with the group in the sentence: 'Of the walkers, 55% play sport.' A column percentage divides by the column total and answers another question: 'Of the players, 29.1% ride.' sources: - title: "Made up for this lesson: the school, the 200 students, how they travel and whether they play sport." url: https://tutorials.learningwaypoints.com/maths/data/row-or-column-percentages/ checked: 2026-10-25 ```

# Dev's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: dev
In the survey, 33 students walk to school and play a sport.
There are 200 students in the survey altogether.
So the percentage of walkers who play sport is 33 out of 200.
33 ÷ 200 = 0.165, which is 16.5%.
So 16.5% of the walkers play sport.
# endregion

# region: mia
I want to know what percentage of riders play sport.
30 riders play sport, and 103 students play sport altogether.
30 ÷ 103 = 0.29, which is about 29%.
So 29% of riders play sport.
# endregion
